Epilepsy, cognition, and mood. Patients with epilep- sy are at increased risk of cognitive and behavioural def- icits. These are often multifactorial in origin: the disease itself and its underlying pathology, psychosocial and envi- ronmental factors, and the effects of antiepileptic treatment may all play a role.1-8 Children are particularly vulnerable: recurrent seizures in the immature brain appear to have an adverse effect on the development of brain structure and function;8 furthermore, behavioural and cognitive deficits may not be detected for a long time, while imposing detri- mental effects on development and learning.4,6 Because of the multifactorial nature of the problem, and the difficul- ties of assessing often subtle changes in cognition, it has proved difficult to study appropriately, and evidence is of- ten scanty. Many studies have been small, and have had methodological flaws.4,6 In addition, there is a need for studies in patient populations at greater risk, such as chil- dren.5,6 There is particular interest in assessing the risks associated with antiepileptic treatment, since it is perhaps the most readily modifiable factor. Strategies such as avoiding unnecessary polytherapy, using the lowest effective dose of an antiepileptic, keeping drug concentrations in thera- peutic ranges, and slow titration when doses are increased, have been associated with fewer cognitive adverse effects. However, it should also be borne in mind that appropriate treatment and good seizure control may offset the negative cognitive effects.4 (There is an interesting suggestion that suppression of interictal discharges in the EEG with lamo- trigine may be associated with an improvement in behav- iour in children with epilepsy and behavioural problems.9) The most common cognitive effects seem to be sedation, somnolence, distractibility, memory impairment, insom- nia, and dizziness; adult patients often experience depres- sion (below), whereas in children hyperactivity and ag- gression may occur.5 More subtle effects on cognitive function and neuropsychological variables also occur. It has proved difficult, for the reasons mentioned above, to establish the comparative severity of cognitive effects be- tween different antiepileptics. However, it seems to be generally agreed that barbiturate antiepileptics such as phenobarbital, and (particularly in the elderly) benzodi- azepines such as clobazam and clonazepam, have the worst profiles, including decreased arousal and deteriora- tion in most areas of cognitive performance;4 in children, phenobarbital may decrease IQ and impair academic achievement.5-7 Other standard antiepileptics such as phenytoin, carbamazepine, and valproate seem to have more modest, and broadly comparable
